title: "Kernel"
description: "A function that measures similarity between data points in a transformed feature space."
term: "Kernel"
letter: "K"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

A kernel is a way to compare two inputs in a richer mathematical space without
explicitly transforming every data point. It is a central idea behind support
vector machines and many kernel methods.

## Technical explanation

A kernel function $K(x, x')$ computes similarity between examples $x$ and $x'$.
Examples include the linear kernel $K(x,x') = x^T x'$, the polynomial kernel,
and the radial basis function (RBF) kernel

$$
K(x,x') = \exp\left(-\gamma \|x-x'\|^2\right).
$$

This lets algorithms work with nonlinear patterns by implicitly evaluating
inner products in a high-dimensional feature space. The actual transformation
is not necessarily computed explicitly.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Kernels enable nonlinear classification and regression while preserving some
computational structure. They are important for classical ML models, feature
engineering, and similarity-based approaches when a linear separator is not
sufficient.

## How it works

Instead of writing out transformed features, the algorithm uses a kernel matrix
that contains pairwise similarities between inputs. This allows it to model
complex relationships while keeping the computation manageable for many
classical methods.

## Practical example

A support vector machine may use an RBF kernel to separate two classes that are
not linearly separable in the original feature space. The kernel allows the
classifier to shape boundaries that capture nonlinear structure.

## Common misconceptions

- A kernel is not the same as a neural-network layer or a learned embedding.
- The kernel function does not always require a human-specified feature map.
- A kernel choice can strongly affect performance, so it should be validated.
